newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan must cut spending before new tax hike -- panel.
newsitem.headline: Japan must cut spending before new tax hike -- panel.

text.p: Japan must cut spending before raising its sales tax beyond a planned five percent increase from April, the head of a government tax panel said on Friday.

"The consumption tax hike to five percent is to make up for the previous tax cuts," Hiroshi Kato told reporters upon the issue of his panel's proposals on the future shape of the tax system. "We accepted this move from the standpoint of giving more leeway in the managing of state finances.
"Further increases must be backed by government efforts. We cannot accept tax increases unless government cuts spending," he said.

On the introduction of a system of consolidated tax payments, under which companies pay taxes on a group basis, including subsidiaries and affiliates, Kato said: "We will carefully consider the introduction of such a system in Japan."
He said the system may be implemented if it clears all the conditions that need to be met, but added that the panel would not make any exceptions.

Industry sources said telecoms giant Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corp was one of the firms eager to see the payment system implemented, having won regulatory approval to set up a holding company to offer international services.
The group payment system means companies in a group can use a loss by another group company to reduce their tax liabilities.
The proposals on the future shape of Japan's tax system were formally adopted by the panel meeting on Friday, and will be reported to Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, Kato said.
The first part of the proposal calls on the public to choose whether it wants "big government" or "small government".
Big government would offer more services but need more taxes. A smaller government would offer less and ask less.
The panel said a new tax system must be fair and simple, and also comply with global standards.
While the share of tax revenues coming from the consumption tax will increase, income tax will remain the main source of government income, it said.

The second part of the proposal listed various opinions on tax reform. For example, it said some felt that corporate taxes should be lowered so that Japanese companies could be more competitive in global markets.
But before lowering corporate taxes, Japan needs to consider how the drop in revenues will be made up, whether by reducing spending or increasing other taxes, the report said.
The government should also review real estate taxes, especially those imposed on land holdings, it said.

Taxes on financial products, on earned interest and on financial transactions should also be reviewed in light of the "Big Bang" financial reforms mapped out by Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, the report said.
